title: Matthew 13:10–17
context: After the Sower parable, the disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables. He answers with the gift of kingdom secrets, Isaiah’s judgment oracle on dull hearts, and a blessing on eyes and ears that truly see and hear—framing how the word divides hearers.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic comment on revelation, hearing, and grace that opens eyes, from both sides of the debate.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: I ascribe to grace the commencement, the continuance and the consummation of all good… The controversy… relates solely to the mode of operation, whether it be irresistible or not… I believe, according to the scriptures, that many persons resist the Holy Spirit and reject the grace that is offered.
The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is FREE IN ALL, and FREE FOR ALL.

reformed.quote: Flesh and blood reveal nothing of this kind… Faith is not formed by the understanding of the flesh, but by the secret revelation of the Spirit.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 16:17)

reformed.quote: I believe the doctrine of election, because I am quite certain that, if God had not chosen me, I should never have chosen Him; and I am sure He chose me before I was born, or else He never would have chosen me afterwards.

verses.text: The disciples came, and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The disciples draw near with a pastoral question: why hide the kingdom in stories for the crowds? They sense that form matters for those still outside the circle of clear teaching.

The note struck is concern for public hearers. Grace that offers the word to many also presses the church to ask how truth is given—so that invitation and clarity remain serious for those who may yet receive.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question marks a turn from crowd to disciples. Jesus will explain His method under the Father’s purpose, not as a technique to maximize applause.

Christ governs how revelation is dispensed. Parables are not a failure of communication but a sovereignly chosen mode that both discloses and judges.

verses.text: He answered them, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus distinguishes gift: secrets of the kingdom have been given to the disciples, not to the resistant crowd in the same way. Knowledge of the kingdom is grace, not native cleverness.

Arminian readers gladly ascribe saving insight to God’s gift—yet typically insist that this grace is sincerely offered more widely, and that hardness often follows resisted light rather than an arbitrary withholding of every opportunity to hear.
verses.reformedNotes:
“It has been given… it has not been given” locates kingdom knowledge in divine donation. Secrets are not seized by flesh; they are bestowed.

Distinguishing grace is true. The Father gives spiritual understanding to whom He will; the same Jesus who invites also discloses that saving knowledge is God’s gift, not human entitlement.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess that kingdom secrets are given, not earned. Arminians press grace that enables a response and warn that persistent refusal dulls further light; Reformed readers emphasize God’s sovereign, effectual granting of knowledge to the elect and withholding of saving insight from the reprobate.

verses.text: For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have abundance; but whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he has.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus states a spiritual economy: receptive hearing receives more; empty, refusing hearing loses even seeming possession. Privilege unused becomes judgment.

Grace enables stewardship of light received. Those who welcome the word grow into abundance; those who neglect or resist find even prior advantages slip away—a sober call to responsible reception.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abundance and loss follow the Lord’s giving. Those who “have” by gift receive more; those who “have not” in saving reality lose even outward hold on truth.

Providence and justice meet here. God’s Word does not leave hearts unchanged—He multiplies light where He has planted life and removes presumptuous claim where there is no true possession.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat this as a serious spiritual principle, not a proverb about luck. Arminians typically tie increase and loss to grace-enabled response or refusal; Reformed readers tie them to God’s sovereign distribution of further light and judicial hardening.

verses.text: Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they don’t see, and hearing, they don’t hear, neither do they understand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Parables meet a people who look without seeing and hear without understanding. Form matches spiritual condition—stories that invite the willing and leave the stubborn without excuse.

Arminians stress culpability: dullness is moral, not merely intellectual. Prevenient grace has granted capacity; refusal to understand remains a blameworthy closing of eyes and ears.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus explains method from spiritual inability: they see and hear outwardly yet do not perceive. Parables both veil and reveal according to the heart’s state under God’s judgment.

Natural sight is not spiritual sight. Without the Spirit’s opening work, crowds remain spectators of truth they do not grasp—even while the Word continues to accomplish God’s purpose.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm blindness and guilt. Arminians highlight resistible grace and responsible dulling of the heart; Calvinists highlight inability cured only by effectual illumination, with parables serving judicial as well as revelatory ends.

verses.text: In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says, ‘By hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive;
verses.arminianNotes:
Isaiah’s oracle lands again: hearing without understanding, seeing without perception. Jesus reads Israel’s tragedy as Scripture fulfilled—not as surprise, but as the outworking of long refusal.

Arminian reading holds God’s foreknowledge and human responsibility together. The prophecy does not annul sincere offers of the word; it exposes a people who keep hearing and will not turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Fulfillment language binds Jesus’ ministry to Isaiah 6. Judicial blindness is not a new idea; it is covenant judgment arriving in the Messiah’s day.

God’s Word never fails of its purpose. Even misunderstood parables fulfill prophecy; sovereignty frames both revelation and the hardening that Scripture foresaw.

verses.text: for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, and they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again, and I would heal them.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The verbs press responsibility: heart grown dull, ears barely hearing, eyes they have closed. Healing stands ready—“I would heal them”—yet they will not turn.

Arminians hear both tragedy and sincerity: God desires healing upon repentance; prevenient grace enables turning; the lest names a self-protective refusal that blocks the cure freely offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Dull heart, heavy ears, closed eyes describe a people under judgment who also act as agents of their own blindness. The lest clause shows aversion to the very healing God would give.

Reformed theology holds guilt and inability together: they close their eyes, and God judicially confirms that path. Healing belongs to those the Lord turns; the text still leaves no room to blame God for their sin.
verses.keyContrast: Both see dullness as culpable and healing as God’s gift upon turning. Arminians press that grace enables a turn and that God sincerely would heal; Reformed interpreters emphasize effectual turning as God’s work and judicial hardening as His righteous response to persistent unbelief.

verses.text: “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear.
verses.arminianNotes:
Blessing flips the oracle: the disciples’ eyes and ears are pronounced happy because they truly see and hear. Privilege is gift, and it calls for grateful stewardship.

Grace has opened them to receive what crowds miss. The beatitude invites all hearers to seek the same opened sight—enabled by grace, answered in faith—rather than presume on nearness to Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes:
“But blessed” marks distinguishing mercy. The same Lord who judges dull hearts blesses seeing eyes and hearing ears among His own.

Spiritual perception is beatitude, not boast. Those who see do so because God has given sight; the blessing rests on gift before it rests on response.

verses.text: For most certainly I tell you that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Prophets and righteous ones longed for this day and did not receive it. The disciples stand in a privileged hour of fulfillment—Messiah present, kingdom secrets unfolding.

Wesleyan Arminians urge humility and urgency: greater light means greater responsibility. Grace that grants what saints of old desired also summons present hearers not to waste the open door.
verses.reformedNotes:
Salvation history peaks here: what prophets longed for, the disciples now see and hear. Redemptive epochs are ordered by God’s decree, not human timetable.

Providence decides when revelation comes. The church inherits sight and hearing as gift in the fullness of time; longing across ages magnifies the mercy now given in Christ.
